exercise.name: Decline Crunch

reference.title: Decline Crunch
reference.listing: Video (title and number from the catalog listing; the page could not be read from this environment, so the movement follows the exercise name and standard coaching)

equipment: Decline bench (slant board with ankle roller)

breathing.pattern: Exhale as you curl up, inhale as you lower.
breathing.cadence: About 0.9 s up, a short pause, about 1.2 s down

prescription.tempo: About 1 s up, brief pause, 1.5 s down
prescription.progression: Steeper board, slower lowering, then a light plate on the chest

cues.text: Lie on the decline board head-down, feet hooked under the roller, fingertips lightly behind the head, elbows wide.
Breathe out and curl the head and shoulder blades off the board; the low back stays down.
Pause with the shoulder blades just off the board.
Breathe in and uncurl back to the board under control.

mistakes.fix: Lift only the shoulder blades; keep the low back on the board.

mistakes.mistake: Pulling the head with the hands

mistakes.fix: Breathe out on the way up.

kinematics.measure: Trunk (pelvis to C7) from the board
kinematics.norm: Shoulder blades just off the board (clinical opinion)
Low back stays on the board (clinical opinion)
Hips barely move in a crunch (Escamilla 2016)

sources.title: Escamilla et al. 2016, muscle activation among supine, prone and side position exercises with and without a Swiss ball (Sports Health 8(4):372-379)
Konrad, Schmitz and Denner 2001, neuromuscular evaluation of trunk-training exercises (J Athl Train 36(2):109-118; PMC155519)
Andersson, Nilsson, Ma and Thorstensson 1997, abdominal and hip flexor muscle activation during various training exercises (Eur J Appl Physiol 75:115-123; PMID 9118976)
Effect of traditional vs modified bent-knee sit-up on abdominal and hip flexor muscle EMG activity (J Strength Cond Res 29(12):3472-3479, 2015; PMID 25970493)
Axler and McGill 1997, low-back loads over a variety of abdominal exercises: searching for the safest abdominal challenge (Med Sci Sports Exerc 29(6):804-811)
McGill 1998, low back exercises: evidence for improving exercise regimens (Phys Ther 78(7):754-765; PMID 9672547)

cautions: Stop if you feel sharp, radiating or nerve-type pain.

Lying head-down raises pressure in the head; skip the decline with uncontrolled high blood pressure, glaucoma or a recent eye or head problem (clinical opinion), and sit up slowly at the end of the set.
Check that the roller is locked and the feet are hooked before lying back.
Full sit-ups load the low back more than curl-ups (McGill 1998; Axler and McGill 1997).
Osteoporosis or vertebral fracture: avoid repeated loaded spinal flexion and twisting.
Muscle glow colours and activation curves are illustrative, not measured EMG.
modify: Neck pain: cross the arms on the chest.
Low-back discomfort: stop at a crunch.

muscleNotes.core: The crunch is mostly rectus abdominis: about 31-38% MVIC in a floor crunch with little hip-flexor work (Escamilla 2016); the decline adds load because the trunk starts head-down.
muscleNotes.obliques: External obliques help curl the trunk (Escamilla 2016).
